newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Victorious Taleban now faces north Afghan warlord.
newsitem.headline: Victorious Taleban now faces north Afghan warlord.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia came face to face with the forces of a powerful northern warlord on Monday after sweeping northward in relentless pursuit of former government forces on Monday.

The Taleban forces claimed victory over key northern towns and a province and said they had entered the strategic Panjsher valley where they had bottled up former defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood after a two-pronged advance overnight from Kabul.
But the Taleban forces, which now control three quarters of the country, halted after forces of the powerful northern Uzbek chief rejected their request to make way, witnesses said.

A United Nations official visiting the area urged the Taleban to negotiate with Dostum rather than fight after the general's forces advanced several km (miles) south from the Soviet-built Salang Tunnel to about three km (two miles) from those of Taleban, reporters visting the area said.

It was not immediately clear whether the Taleban, who conquered the capital Kabul on Friday, wanted the passage through the famous Salang Highway to attack some northern provinces still held by forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani or wanted to capture Dostum's territory.

Dostum has so far stayed away from the fighting between Taleban and the former Kabul government, which he also opposed. In recent months, Rabbani has been trying to strike an alliance with Dostum while Taleban also said after taking Kabul that it wanted to settle important matters with him through talks.

A Taleban commander, Mullah Ghulam Mohammad, told reporters the Taleban had asked Dostum's forces to make way for them, but the request had been rejected. "We told them to let the Taleban cross because Dostum does not represent the north," he said.

Earlier, the militia was halted at the village of Golbahar at the mouth of the narrow gorge leading into Panjsher after a steady advance from Charikar, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, through to nearby Jabal os-Siraj, fighters said.

But a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), quoted Taleban sources as saying that the militia had taken Golbahar and then gone five to six km (three to four miles) into Panjsher -- one of the few areas still under the control of the government which the Taleban ousted last week.
A second prong pushed north from Jabal os-Siraj, up the Salang highway that runs north from Kabul into central Asia.
The fighters in Golbahar said Taleban troops had reached the southern end of a major tunnel on the highway.
They also said that had moved significant forces into the area north of the Salang tunnel, which crosses the formidable Hindu Kush mountain range, over the past few days.
Taleban sources quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said that Kapisa province to the east of Golbahar and its capital Mahmud-i-Raqi had fallen to the militia on Monday.
Mohammad Gul, deputy Taleban commander of a military barracks near Kabul, said the militia planned to seize all the territory held by the former government.
"We intend to capture all the former government areas, including the Salang tunnel and the Panjsher," he said.

However it was not immediately clear how easy it would be for the Taleban to capture the valley, held by Masood's men throughout the 1980s against several major assaults by Soviet troops backing Kabul's then-communist government.
The speed of his retreat -- from Kabul to the valley in just three days -- seemed to have dismayed the Tajik people he leads.

"We just don't know what's happening. We don't know whether Masood has a plan or is just running," said one ethnic Tajik shopkeeper in Golbahar as a jeepload of Taleban fighters swept past in a cloud of dust.
News of the advances set nerves on edge around Mazar-i-Sharif, an important trading centre in the far north controlled by Dostum.
Officials with his well-armed Jumbish-i-Milli faction said they were ready to fight.
"We don't want to join this war," said a senior Jumbish official who declined to be named. "But if they (the Taleban) attack, we would defend ourselves."
The Taleban set up an interim ruling council vowing to turn Afghanistan into an Islamic state soon after taking Kabul.
It has begun enforcing a fundamentalist brand of Islam that has struck fear into many educated people, especially women.
